content: 1. Patients should be actively involved in decisions regarding their treatment, with their medical, psychosocial, and spiritual status being central to these decisions. 2. Access to palliative care and essential medicines, including opioid analgesics like morphine, is a fundamental component of the right to health and well-being, as outlined by the United Nations international drug control conventions. 3. Palliative care is an ethical responsibility of health systems, and healthcare professionals have a duty to alleviate pain and suffering—whether physical, psychosocial, or spiritual—regardless of whether the underlying disease is curable. End-of-life care is a critical aspect of palliative care. 4. More than 40 million people require palliative care annually, and this need is expected to grow due to aging populations and the increasing prevalence of chronic and noncommunicable diseases. 5. Palliative care for children is particularly important, and Member States should estimate the quantities of internationally controlled medicines needed, including pediatric formulations. 6. Palliative care must be integrated across the continuum of care, especially at the primary care level, as inadequate integration contributes to inequitable access to such care. 7. Many countries face insufficient availability and use of internationally controlled medicines for pain and symptom relief, highlighting the need for Member States to address regulatory barriers while preventing misuse and diversion. 8. The lack of knowledge about palliative care perpetuates avoidable suffering, emphasizing the need for ongoing education and training for healthcare providers, caregivers, and family members. 9. Palliative care employs an interdisciplinary approach to address the needs of patients and their families. Strong networks between professional palliative care providers, support care providers, volunteers, and families are essential for delivering quality care. 10. Palliative care is needed across all age groups and disease categories, including noncommunicable diseases, infectious diseases, HIV, and multidrug-resistant tuberculosis. 11. Palliative care is now included in the definition of universal health coverage, and health services must provide integrated and equitable palliative care to meet patients' needs. 12. Adequate funding mechanisms for palliative care programs, including medicines and medical products, are crucial, particularly in developing countries. 13. The inclusion of palliative care actions and indicators in the WHO global monitoring framework for noncommunicable diseases is a significant step forward. 14. The WHO Model List of Essential Medicines now includes medicines for pain and symptom control in palliative care settings, which is a commendable effort to improve access. 15. Non-governmental organizations and civil society play a vital role in advocating for palliative care and ensuring the availability and appropriate use of controlled substances for medical purposes. 16. Member States are urged to develop and implement palliative care policies that integrate evidence-based, cost-effective, and equitable services across all levels of care, with a focus on primary, community, and home-based care. 17. Domestic funding and human resources should be allocated to palliative care initiatives, including policy development, education, training, and quality improvement. 18. Basic training in palliative care should be included in undergraduate medical and nursing education, as well as in-service training for primary care providers. 19. Intermediate training should be provided to healthcare workers who routinely care for patients with life-threatening illnesses, such as those in oncology, infectious diseases, pediatrics, geriatrics, and internal medicine. 20. Specialist palliative care training should be available for professionals managing complex symptom management needs. 21. National essential medicines lists should be updated to include pain and palliative care medicines, reflecting recent additions to the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines. 22. Partnerships between governments and civil society, including patient organizations, should be fostered to support palliative care services. 23. Palliative care actions included in the WHO global action plan for noncommunicable diseases should be implemented and monitored. 24. The WHO Director-General is requested to ensure that palliative care is integrated into global disease control and health system plans, including those for noncommunicable diseases and universal health coverage. 25. Evidence-based guidelines and tools on palliative care, including pain management for adults and children, should be developed and disseminated. 26. National health systems should integrate palliative care across disease groups and levels of care, addressing ethical issues such as equitable access, person-centered care, and community involvement. 27. The WHO Access to Controlled Medicines Programme should support Member States in reviewing and improving national legislation and policies to balance the prevention of misuse and ensuring access to controlled medicines. 28. Efforts should be made to increase the availability and accessibility of palliative care medicines through collaboration with Member States, networks, civil society, and international stakeholders. 29. The WHO should work with the International Narcotics Control Board, the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime, and health ministries to promote balanced control of controlled medicines for pain and symptom management. 30. Research on effective palliative care models in lowand middle-income countries should be encouraged, with a focus on good practices. 31. Progress in implementing palliative care initiatives should be reported to the World Health Assembly.
